analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.50 an hour in three annual steps.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $6.50 an hour never left committee and died without a vote at the end of the 105th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage beyond the $5.15 level set in 1996: to $5.50 an hour starting July 1998, $6.00 starting July 1999, and $6.50 starting July 2000. Roughly matching a phased increase in the wage floor, it would have lifted pay for millions of hourly workers. It was introduced in February 1997, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers paid at or near the minimum wage, including many fast-food, retail, and cleaning workers, would have seen their pay rise in steps to $6.50 an hour. The bill also raised the subminimum 'tipped' framework by lifting the base rate under the same law, so workers whose tips were counted toward the minimum would share in the increase.

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrote the wage floor in the Fair Labor Standards Act to $5.50 an hour beginning July 1, 1998, $6.00 an hour beginning July 1, 1999, and $6.50 an hour beginning July 1, 2000 — a rise of $1.35 over the $5.15 rate then in effect.
Every worker covered by the federal minimum wage would have legally been owed the higher rates, which is most hourly workers in retail, food service, and other low-wage jobs.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay low wages — restaurants, retail stores, hotels, and other businesses that rely on minimum-wage labor — would have faced higher payroll costs, and some economists argued that could mean fewer entry-level jobs or higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Raising the wage floor by $1.35 over three years would raise labor costs for businesses that employ many minimum-wage workers, and opponents of minimum-wage increases argue this can reduce entry-level hiring or push prices up for customers.
A federal increase applies uniformly across high-cost and low-cost states, so the same $6.50 rate is a bigger change relative to wages in lower-wage regions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a straightforward, phased raise for the country's lowest-paid workers, at a cost concentrated on low-wage employers. Research on minimum-wage increases remains contested, but the direct effect on millions of paychecks would have been large and immediate, while the cost fell on a smaller, better-organized set of employers. The bill's fatal weakness was political: with only 22 sponsors, all Democrats or independents, it had no path out of a committee led by the opposing party.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat until Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Olver introduced the Fair Wage Act of 1997 on February 11, 1997, with 11 original co-introducers including Rep. Bernie Sanders.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On March 14, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was ever taken.
A total of 21 members cosponsored the bill — 20 Democrats and 1 independent — and the committee never acted on it before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
The bill's proposed schedule built on the $5.15 minimum wage that took effect September 1, 1997 under a 1996 law; Congress in this session did not raise the wage floor further.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage employers such as restaurants and retail chains came out ahead, because the wage floor stayed at $5.15 and they avoided the scheduled increases. Minimum-wage workers gained nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. John W. Olver
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited co-introducers including Sanders, Conyers, Frank, and Gutierrez.

for.name: Rep. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Representative, Vermont; independent, original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Was one of the original co-introducers of the bill.

for.name: 21 cosponsors (20 Democrats, 1 independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them chaired a committee with power to move it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. William Goodling (R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a markup or advanced the bill.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.role: Subcommittee of referral within Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 14, 1997 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent — 20 Democrats and 1 independent — and with Republicans holding the House majority and the committee chairmanship, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The industry employs more minimum-wage workers than almost any other and would have absorbed the wage increases directly. Its interest in keeping the floor at $5.15 ran against the pay raise workers would have received.

industries.industry: Retail, hospitality, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Businesses that staff entry-level positions at or near the minimum wage would have faced higher payroll costs under the three-step increase to $6.50.
